articles.headline: The Labour party has lost the plot on net zero | Letters
articles.teaser: Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta FahnbullehWatching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero (Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war.Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies, which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry.
articles.originalHeadline: The Labour party has lost the plot on net zero | Letters

articles.headline: The British Library is wrong to repurpose its reading rooms | Letters
articles.teaser: To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as ‘evidence’ is unworthy of our world-class research institution, says Marcia SaundersAfter a cyber-attack in 2023, which Ciaran Martin, a former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, described as “one of the worst cyber incidents in British history”, use of the British Library’s reading rooms fell dramatically (British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces, 20 November).Throughout 2024-25, services were heavily affected, including archives, manuscripts, books and online journal articles. All readers’ tickets were suspended and initially were reissued for limited periods of time. It should surprise no one that use of the reading rooms fell off. Only last month was access to the UK web archive (partially) restored.
articles.originalHeadline: The British Library is wrong to repurpose its reading rooms | Letters

articles.headline: London Museum’s donors and the capital’s dubious domination | Letters
articles.teaser: Omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that ‘magisterial’ civic amenities just happen by magic, writes Beth Breeze. Plus letters from Rendel Harris and Tom UprichardOliver Wainwright’s extremely positive review of the “magisterial” new London Museum will encourage many to visit (Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight, 24 November).But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. In particular, omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that fantastic civic amenities just happen by magic, or are totally funded by taxpayers.
articles.originalHeadline: London Museum’s donors and the capital’s dubious domination | Letters

articles.headline: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
articles.teaser: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young peopleThis should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s.
articles.originalHeadline: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee

articles.headline: The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people | Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: Milburn’s review doesn’t ask what kind of work young people will be going into: zero hours, minimum wage, mind-numbing. Do we have the guts to solve that?One big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government.Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself.

articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
articles.originalHeadline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
